policy: Review every closed candidate set. Select only when ASV wording or an explicit mapped textual note distinguishes a reading; otherwise mark underdetermined and retain the base fallback. The base candidate is the qere, which is what MACULA Hebrew projects; the alternative is the ketiv written in the Leningrad Codex.

decisions.evidence: ASV renders a singular subject throughout the clause chain: 'he that entereth ... shall go forth ... he shall not return ... but shall go forth straight before him.' The qere singular yetse' matches; the ketiv plural yets'u would give 'they shall go forth.' ASV wording distinguishes the reading.

ASV opens the verse with no rendered conjunction: 'Thus shall they prepare the lamb.' The ketiv we'asu writes an initial waw, which ASV renders as 'And' at the head of a verse as a matter of course in this chapter's narrative and legislative sequence; the qere ya'asu has none. The absence of 'And' distinguishes the qere.

ASV reads 'there was a place on the hinder part westward,' with no number or possessive that would separate the readings: the qere dual bayyarkhathayim and the ketiv biyrkhatham ('in their hinder part') are both carried by the same English phrase, and ASV supplies no possessive pronoun and no plural. No ASV note is mapped to this unit. Base fallback (qere) carries the projection.
